summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for monitoring running instances of RObust Header Compression (ROHC), a technique that shrinks packet headers on slow or lossy links. It provides statistics and settings such as the profiles in use and compression performance.

plainLanguage.summary: Packets carry long labels on every box. Header compression writes a short nickname instead. This document defines how a manager checks how well the nickname trick is working.

subtitle: SNMP MIB modules for watching Robust Header Compression instances, channels, profiles and contexts.

tldr.problem: Robust Header Compression (ROHC) shrinks packet headers on links such as wireless channels, but operators had no standard way to see which instances, profiles and contexts were running or how well they compressed.
tldr.mechanism: Three MIB modules expose ROHC instances, channels, profiles and per-flow contexts through SNMP, with a general module shared by all profiles and small profile-specific modules.
tldr.outcome: Operators can check configuration, state, mode and compression statistics with SNMP. It is a Proposed Standard and only two objects are writable.

today: RFC 3816 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What ROHC Is and What This MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 3816 describes managed objects for monitoring running instances of RObust Header Compression (ROHC), which is defined in RFC 3095. ROHC is a framework for IP header compression that lets the compression efficiency be traded against robustness to channel errors, depending on the channel.

Compressors and decompressors sit at the end points of channels. They exploit the fact that successive packet headers in a flow are similar: non-changing fields and reference values of predictable fields are kept as context. Once the decompressor has the same context, only delta information and unpredictable fields have to be sent.

The MIB is written in SMIv2 and accessed through SNMP, as described in RFC 3410. The RFC says the objects support configuration management, fault management and performance monitoring.
sections.plainLanguage: If you send the same long address on every letter, you can agree on a short nickname once and use that after. ROHC does this for packet headers, and this MIB lets a manager check it is working.

sections.title: Three Modules for General and Profile-Specific Data
sections.content:
The MIB follows the ROHC architecture of RFC 3759. ROHC is expected to grow, so the objects are split into three modules. ROHC-MIB covers things shared by all profiles. ROHC-UNCOMPRESSED-MIB covers the uncompressed profile 0x0000 from RFC 3095. ROHC-RTP-MIB covers the RTP (0x0001), UDP (0x0002) and ESP (0x0003) profiles from RFC 3095 and the Link Layer Assisted (LLA) profile 0x0005 from RFC 3242.

The profiles in the RTP module were found to be tightly related, so one joint module was preferred to individual ones. The RFC notes that a TCP profile was under development and SCTP compression was being discussed, and that future profiles can each get a small module of their own.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one general checklist for everything, and a few small extra checklists for each special kind of compression. New kinds can bring their own extra checklist.

sections.title: Channels, Instances and Profiles
sections.content:
All tables in ROHC-MIB are indexed by the IP interface number and a numeric channel identifier. The rohcChannelTable lists the channels used for compressed packets or for feedback from decompressor to compressor, each with a type (notInUse, rohc or dedicatedFeedback), a description string and an enabled or disabled status.

The rohcInstanceTable describes compressor and decompressor instances. An instance is tied to exactly one channel, but the instance type (compressor or decompressor) is also part of the index so that all compressors can be listed without touching any decompressor. Its properties include vendor, version, clock resolution, MAX_CID, the LARGE_CIDS flag, the MRRU and the storage time for contexts. Optional statistics include flow counts, packet counts, IR and IR-DYN counts and the total compression ratio.

The rohcProfileTable lists the profiles available at each instance, with the profile number, vendor and version, a description, and a flag showing whether the profile has been negotiated with the other end.
sections.plainLanguage: One list names the roads that carry squeezed packets. Another lists the squeezing machines at the ends. A third lists which squeezing tricks each machine knows.

sections.title: Contexts, State and Mode
sections.content:
The rohcContextTable has one row per compressor or decompressor context, identified by instance and context identifier (CID). A new context creates a new row. After a context expires or terminates, its row stays until the storage time runs out or the CID is reused. The state of a CID is unused, active, expired or terminated.

Optional context statistics cover activation and deactivation time, packets sent or received, IRs, IR-DYNs and feedbacks, decompressor failures and repairs, compression ratios, and mean compressed packet and header sizes. Several of these are also given over the last 16 packets.

The profile modules extend this table. rohcUncmprContextTable gives the compressor state and mode for profile 0x0000. rohcRtpContextTable gives state and mode for the RTP, UDP, ESP and LLA profiles, with optional ACK, NACK and SNACK counters. The optional packet size table lists allowed packet sizes, or preferred sizes for LLA.

A compression ratio is defined as 1000 times the compressed bytes divided by the original bytes, rounded to the next integer. It can exceed 1000 because compressed data can be larger than the original.
sections.plainLanguage: Each squeezed conversation gets a numbered file card. The MIB keeps the card for a while after the conversation ends, then throws it away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only two objects are writable: rohcInstanceContextStorageTime and rohcContextStorageTime, which set how long context information is kept after a context ends. Setting them too low, such as zero, can lose information about past contexts. Setting them very high can make the agent use a lot of memory. The RFC says unauthorized access to them cannot harm existing ROHC connections or allow malicious manipulation of running instances.

Readable objects could expose information about existing sessions, though the only thing that might be disclosed is the use of channels. Users and addresses are not visible in the MIB. The RFC still recommends controlling GET and notification access, and it RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with cryptographic security. Earlier SNMP versions are NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost everything is look-only. The two things you can change only decide how long old file cards are kept, so mistakes there cannot break the live connections.
